paper_title: Every Pixel Is an Option: A System One Model for Medical Ultrasound Biometry

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: **Purpose:** Ultrasound biometry is widely used across various clinical applications, including prenatal and cardiac examinations, to obtain quantitative measurements by placing calipers at anatomical landmarks. However, these measurements remain subject to interoperator variability as they rely largely on manual caliper placement. Conventional methods often use specialized prediction heads for different ultrasound tasks, whereas vision-language models offer flexibility through text instructions. However, direct coordinate prediction does not explicitly model spatial likelihood distributions, limiting the representation of localization ambiguity. **Methods:** We propose Kev-Bio, a vision-language model that uses clinical measurement questions to guide ultrasound landmark detection. Inspired by System One decision models, Kev-Bio uses decision representations of the language model to generate queries for each caliper endpoint. These queries are matched against shared dense ultrasound features to produce spatial probability maps, from which landmark coordinates and clinical measurements are derived. The model is trained end-to-end using both landmark localization and clinical measurement losses. **Results:** On the nine-view FU/GU Biometry 2026 dataset, Kev-Bio achieves a mean radial error (MRE) of 22.50 pixels and a clinical measurement mean absolute error (MAE) of 15.38, outperforming the compared baselines in overall performance. **Conclusion:** These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Kev-Bio for ultrasound landmark detection and clinical measurement across different anatomical views. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/Kev-Bio.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Ultrasound is widely used to examine anatomy during routine care and to guide clinical procedures. It provides real-time images without exposing patients to ionizing radiation [1]. Beyond visual assessment, many clinical examinations also require quantitative measurements of anatomical structures. These measurements are obtained by placing calipers at predefined landmarks and calculating distances, angles, or circumferences. Choosing the correct points requires knowledge of both anatomy and the measurement protocol. Although standardized training can yield high reproducibility, measurements can still differ between observers [2]. Automatic caliper placement could reduce this manual effort and make quantitative assessment more consistent [3]. landmark localization remains challenging in ultrasound imaging. Speckle noise, acoustic shadowing, and indistinct tissue boundaries can obscure anatomical structures, while changes in probe orientation alter their appearance. single ultrasound image may support multiple clinical measurements, each requiring distinct set of landmarks. Models developed for these tasks commonly use shared image encoder with separate decoders or landmark-specific parameters [4]. Although these architectures can localize predefined landmarks, each measurement task remains tied to fixed output head or task-specific parameter set, making adaptation to new anatomical structures or measurement tasks challenging.

sections.title: Accurate anatomical
sections.content: Previous studies have used multimodal language models to predict segmentation masks and point locations from text and image representations [5, 6]. Ultrasound biometry, however, requires precise localization of multiple measurement endpoints, whose anatomical roles vary across tasks. The central challenge is to identify which endpoints clinical instruction refers to and locate each endpoint accurately in the image within shared framework. Recent System One models, such as Jev [7] and its open-weight counterpart Kev [8], formulate prediction as scoring candidate responses rather than generating answers autoregressively. While primarily explored for decision-support tasks, this formulation offers potential for spatial localization by treating image locations as candidate responses to clinical localization questions. Building on this insight, we introduce Kev-Bio, unified framework that translates clinical measurement questions into landmark queries and grounds them in dense ultrasound features to localize anatomical landmarks. Specifically, we initialize Qwen3.5 with Kev [8, 9] to interpret the ultrasound image and measurement instructions, generating queries for the required anatomical landmarks. These queries interact with shared dense feature map combining representations from Qwen3.5, USFM, and DINOv2 [911] to produce landmark probability maps. The maps provide spatial information about localization ambiguity, while joint landmark and measurement supervision guides training. We evaluate this formulation across nine ultrasound views through comparisons with established methods and controlled ablation studies.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Landmark detection in medical images. Landmark detectors commonly predict coordinates or heatmaps at predefined anatomical points. nnLandmark provides self-configuring approach to three-dimensional landmark detection, while MedSapiens adapts pose estimation representations to medical images [12, 13]. For ultrasound biometry, CAMS and IMPACT-L combine shared image encoders with decoders specific to each task [4, 14]. Echo-CoPilot illustrates the use of learned measurement tools in broader system for echocardiographic interpretation [15]. Our method instead derives endpoint queries from the representation of clinical measurement question. Language models and spatial prediction. LISA uses language model state to predict segmentation masks, while recent point grounding work predicts heatmaps from multimodal representations [5, 6]. We build on this connection between language and spatial prediction, but focus on groups of caliper points whose geometry defines clinical measurement. Kev is an open decision model trained on Qwen3.5 [8]. We initialize the Qwen3.5 language model with the pretrained Kev adapter and train separate pixel pointer to localize ultrasound landmarks.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Let be an ultrasound image of width and height H, with known anatomical view v. Each view has predefined set of clinical measurements M(v), where each measurement M(v) is associated with clinical question tm and the number of required anatomical landmarks is Km {2, 3, 4}. Kev-Bio predicts these landmarks and computes the corresponding measurements from their coordinates. As illustrated in Figure 1, the model combines multimodal language model with shared dense visual feature map. The language model produces decision representation for each measurement, which is then transformed into endpoint-specific queries for locating landmarks in the feature map.

Their visual tokens are denoted by Q(I) and (I), respectively. The USFM tokens are projected into the language models embedding space using learned projection network PU . The input also includes view instruction tv describing the anatomical view and clinical domain, followed by clinical measurement question tm for each measurement M(v). sections.title: 3.4 Heatmap and Measurement Supervision
sections.content: The predicted landmarks for measurement are passed to measurement-specific geometric function to calculate biometric value, ˆym = gm(ˆpm,1, . . . , ˆpm,Km). The geometric function computes distance, an angle, or circumference approximation from the corresponding calipers depending on the measurement. Training jointly supervises the predicted landmark coordinates, their spatial probability maps, and the clinical measurement values calculated from these coordinates. The pointer loss Lptr calculates the L1 error between predicted and ground-truth landmark coordinates and normalizes it by the image diagonal length. The heatmap loss Lhm calculates the cross-entropy between the predicted spatial probability map and normalized Gaussian distribution centered at the ground-truth landmark. This transforms point-based landmark supervision into continuous probability field, encouraging high confidence near the true location while allowing spatial uncertainty around it. The geometric loss Lgeom calculates the absolute error between the predicted and ground-truth measurement values and normalizes it by the training-set median of the corresponding measurement. sections.title: 4.1 Dataset and Implementation Details
sections.content: We evaluate Kev-Bio on the FU/GU Biometry 2026 benchmark, introduced at the MICCAI 2026 FoundUS challenge [16]. The dataset spans nine ultrasound views across three clinical domains: cardiac, prenatal, and intrapartum imaging  (Table 1)  . The labelled benchmark contains 6,743 images, with 60 view-specific landmark definitions and 29 clinical measurements. These measurements include distances, ellipse circumferences, and angles, with each view requiring between one and eleven measurements. The dataset is highly imbalanced, ranging from 38 labelled images for IVC to 4,000 for AoP. An additional 191,170 unlabelled frames are provided but are not used in our experiments. Since the official challenge test annotations are unavailable for offline evaluation, we perform five-fold cross-validation on the labelled data, with approximately 1,350 images held out per fold. All methods are trained and evaluated using the same partitions. We initialize the language backbone from Kev [8], based on Qwen3.5-0.8B, and finetune it with LoRA adapters (r=16). The Qwen vision encoder and USFM are adapted with rank-16 LoRA, while DINOv2 ViT-L/14 uses rank-32. We set λhm = 0.1, λgeom = 6 0.2, and λaux = 1 and train for 24 epochs using AdamW with weight decay of 0.05 and an effective batch size of 8. Learning rates are 103 for newly initialized modules, 104 for the language model and DINOv2 adapters, and 5 105 for the remaining adapters. For all methods and baselines, we adopt the publicly released codebases and corresponding pretrained model weights. Training samples are drawn uniformly across the nine views, with photometric and affine augmentations following [17]. All experiments were conducted on NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80 GB GPU memory).

sections.title: 4.2 Comparison with Prior Methods
sections.content: We compare Kev-Bio with two general-purpose landmark detectors, nnLandmark [12] and MedSapiens [13], and four methods developed for the FU/GU Biometry challenge: CAMS [14], IMPACT-L [4], FMUB [18], and US-Foundation [17]. We report mean radial error (MRE) for landmark localization and mean absolute error (MAE) for clinical measurements, both in pixels (degrees for AoP) averaged across the nine views. As shown in Table 2, Kev-Bio achieves the lowest average error on both metrics among the reported methods, with 22.50 pixels MRE and 15.38 MAE, compared with 23.88 and 17.47 for the strongest respective baselines. It achieves the best landmark localization on eight of the nine views and the lowest measurement error on six, spanning both cardiac and prenatal imaging, with comparable parameter count. The improvement is particularly notable in fetal head biometry, where MRE decreases from 17.03 to 13.76 pixels. Notably, these results are obtained without using the additional unlabelled challenge data leveraged by CAMS and FMUB. Although competing methods achieve slightly lower measurement errors on femur length, cervical length, and angle of progression, Kev-Bio maintains the lowest average error across both metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness across diverse anatomical views and measurement tasks.

sections.title: 4.3 Qualitative Results
sections.content: Figure 2 presents qualitative comparisons between Kev-Bio and US-Foundation [17] across all nine ultrasound views. Kev-Bio places most landmarks closer to their annotated anatomical targets, whereas US-Foundation shows larger localization errors, including predictions on neighboring structures. This is particularly evident in the IVC, fetal head, and femur examples, where substantial localization errors are observed for US-Foundation despite accurate predictions from Kev-Bio. In the A4C example containing adjacent cardiac views, Kev-Bio correctly identifies the target anatomy, while US-Foundation places several landmarks on the neighboring view. These examples illustrate the ability of text-conditioned spatial pointing to preserve anatomical correspondence across diverse ultrasound measurements. Beyond landmark localization, Kev-Bio produces spatial probability map for each endpoint (Figure 3a), whose entropy serves as an uncertainty score. To assess whether this score identifies localization failures, we consider predictions more than 5% of the image diagonal from ground truth as errors. We then rank predictions by decreasing entropy and measure the fraction of errors captured among the highest-ranked predictions (Figure 3b). These results suggest that Kev-Bios probability maps can help clinicians identify caliper placements that warrant closer inspection, enabling more targeted verification of automated measurements. Finally, Figure 4 visualizes how clinical questions guide spatial localization. Given the same ultrasound image, different measurement questions produce distinct probability maps that concentrate on the corresponding anatomical landmarks. In A4C, for example, queries for ventricular length and atrial width highlight different anatomical endpoints, while related fetal head measurements yield consistent responses at shared landmarks. These observations illustrate how Kev-Bio adapts its spatial predictions to different measurement definitions through shared, question-conditioned pixel pointer.

sections.title: 4.4 Ablation Study
sections.content: We assess the contribution of each component by retraining model variants under identical settings, as reported in Table 3. Removing the pixel pointer (replacing spatial localization with direct coordinate regression from the decision states) leads to the largest performance degradation, increasing MRE from 22.50 to 35.50 pixels and MAE from 15.38 to 23.64. This highlights the importance of matching measurementspecific queries to dense spatial features rather than directly regressing coordinates 8 Fig. 2 Qualitative comparison across nine ultrasound views. Landmark predictions from Kev-Bio (red) and US-Foundation (blue), with ground truth shown in green. Values indicate mean landmark error in pixels. from the decision states. Removing DINOv2 also reduces performance, yielding 24.85 MRE and 16.94 MAE, indicating the benefit of complementary visual representations for precise landmark localization. Excluding the language model (LLM) and replacing its decision states with learned, image-conditioned measurement queries results in smaller but consistent increase in error (23.66 MRE and 16.77 MAE), suggesting that language-conditioned queries contribute to localization accuracy even when measurement definitions are fixed. sections.title: 5 Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: Kev-Bio offers unified approach to ultrasound biometry by handling different clinical measurements through shared localization framework, as opposed to task-specific prediction heads. Beyond predicting landmark coordinates, its spatial probability maps provide information about ambiguous predictions, potentially helping clinicians 9 Fig. 3 Spatial probability maps and error detection. (a) Landmark probability maps showing confident and ambiguous predictions. (b) Landmarks are ranked by decreasing map entropy, and curves show the fraction of localization errors captured in each clinical domain. Errors are defined using ground truth as deviations exceeding 5% of the image diagonal. The black marker indicates the overall result, and the dashed line represents random selection. Fig. 4 Question-conditioned landmark localization. Different clinical measurement questions produce distinct landmark probability maps on the same ultrasound image. Green circles denote ground truth, and yellow regions indicate predicted spatial distributions. identify caliper placements that require verification. Nevertheless, our evaluation is limited to predefined measurements on single benchmark, despite spanning multiple anatomical regions. Generalization to unseen measurement instructions, anatomical structures, and different imaging conditions remains to be explored. Future work will investigate these directions, alongside uncertainty calibration and computational efficiency.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Kev-Bio, System One framework that formulates medical ultrasound biometry as spatial decision-making. By grounding clinical measurement questions in dense visual features, the model localizes anatomical landmarks and derives clinical measurements within unified framework. Experiments across nine ultrasound views demonstrate improvements over existing methods, while the predicted probability maps provide additional information about localization ambiguity.
